Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. Gulin Qingmao uses 'If it stays, it is not alike; if it is alike, it does not stay' in two different compositions, leaving what is to stay or resemble something unstated. In a poem on a portrait of Chuanzi, he invokes the oar as a livelihood, bait on the hook though no fish is in the water, and three nods that leave no room for discussion. He ends by asking where Chuanzi went when he overturned the boat. The paired refusal unsettles the picture's attempt to hold its subject in place; Chuanzi is the depicted figure, while Gulin is the poem's speaker. The verse does not provide a fixed portrait-identification test or a literal answer about where Chuanzi can now be found.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1413.xml). Supplementary Gathas and Verses of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. Sending the monk Hui to travel in Zhejiang, Gulin first invokes the three essentials and three mysteries, responsive use, distinct guest and host, and the whole activity emerging and withdrawing without obstruction. He places the headword after that freedom, then turns to Zhejiang's clear water and white rice: eating them should bring shame and self-scrutiny, while even the exalted eye must answer to taking up a spoon and setting down chopsticks. The farewell asks that the traveler not settle into a fixed resemblance to accomplished practice; its final ordinary actions keep the grand vocabulary accountable to daily conduct.

Senses.Note: Miyun Yuanwu raises a two-pair Perfect Awakening Sutra quotation in the hall, asks where Buddha is working, rejects a monk's reply and strikes him. The selected second pair is Buddha's quoted teaching; Miyun uses it to press the live exchange. Buddha is the inherited scriptural speaker; Zhanran gives the current application. These are two independent present uses; evidence depth remains provisional. In a small-group instruction, Azi Jinwu quotes the Perfect Awakening Sutra after warning that even great wisdom can have a dark patch. He interprets the pair as a Chan test of meeting delusive thought without adding another act of knowing. The selected words are the locally marked scripture quotation; Azi supplies the present explanation. In a hall talk at Baoen, Dachuan Puji revoices the inherited scripture pair in his own unmarked verse, saying it cannot be squeezed into a lump or pried open. Senses.Explanation: To reside on a mountain is to live at, or take responsibility for, a mountain monastery or hermitage. Fachang Yiyu asks whether Ying's reply accords with the business of mountain residence, while Mazu Daoyi tells Yaoshan Weiyan to bind his belly and go reside wherever he can. Hansong Zhicao turns flight from reputation into the line, ‘I intended to flee fame and live in the mountains, but the fame of living on a mountain instead went out among people.’ The unnamed Three-Dou Hermit invokes his long residence to explain having no sitting mat, and Ouyang Xiu asks an old monk how long he has lived there.

Senses.Explanation: Fix the mind and contemplate stillness names holding the mind in place while taking quiet as what is to be observed. The Platform record puts the wording in Zhicheng's report of Shenxiu's instruction; Huineng immediately calls it an illness rather than Zen and questions the value of prolonged sitting. Wanfeng Shiwei groups it with raising the mind to look outward, gathering the mind to clarify inwardly, and congealing the mind to enter the Way. Songyuan Chongyue quotes Linji Yixuan condemning the same four-part list. Tianran Hanshi likewise questions the difference between prolonged sitting and taking this as final. Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the rank “absolute within the relative” (偏中正) names the absolute or upright disclosed within the relative or differentiated, reversing the nesting of “relative within the absolute” while remaining paired with it in explanations and verse sequences. Caoshan Benji glosses the rank as leaving affairs and entering principle. The Eyes of Humans and Devas transmits the same affairs-to-principle gloss in its Five Ranks account. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the rank a sea-cloud, sacred-peak, returning-traveler, and mirror image. Langting Ting pairs it with a yellow bird carrying spring news. Juelang Daosheng associates it with a western circle and lesser yin, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies the same shout as this rank when it is silent right where it occurs. Tianran Hanshi reports Dongshan's old-woman-and-mirror stanza and answers it with another mirror verse; the varied images illustrate rather than define the relation.

Senses.Explanation: The side position is the differentiated member of Caodong positional language: it is where forms, speech, and responsive activity are located in contrast with the straight position. Caoshan Benji identifies it with the realm in which myriad forms appear, then turns that classification into an interview test when an unnamed monastic interlocutor claims to come from the side position. Linquan Conglun preserves the refusal in his appraisal. Yongjue Yuanxian classifies merit and royal-son sequences as matters on this side while warning against mechanically mapping separate schemes together. Baiyu and Dahui Zonggao both expose a limit: diagrams and verbal explanations can themselves remain side-position talk. The term therefore names a relational position inside these attested schemes; it is not a general synonym for error, inferiority, or one physical side.

Senses.Note: The pair can name Caodong positions, but the records also use it more broadly for a distinction that speech or perception may make, miss, or coordinate.

Senses.Note: Asked how to teach where two devices do not reach, Tong'an says that the matter is not met in a partial position and is not lost within the hidden. Zhe'an and Danxia answer the case in separate verses; Linquan says the question itself caught the monk in a set of positions. Much later Yuanjie uses the same line to ask how to meet in a proper position. Pinjixiang judges that exchange and asks for another path. The paired terms test a listener's reliance on named positions.

Senses.Note: Jinfeng contrasts two ways he answered students over twenty years. Earlier he answered ordinary and holy questions on their own terms; later he says he no longer does so. The pair names that later refusal to remain inside the categories supplied by the question. Pofeng and Tian’an reverse which phase counts as compassionate teaching, while Foyuan, Qibai, and Jingting challenge what Jinfeng’s contrast really accomplishes. An answer must work in the encounter, rather than merely follow a rule about ordinary or holy labels.

Senses.Note: Jinfeng says that twenty years earlier he had grandmotherly concern: when asked about ordinary matters he answered ordinarily, and when asked about holy matters he answered accordingly. He then describes a later practice of refusing those expected answers. Tianyin asks whether either period escapes the ordinary and holy divide. Tian’an and Pofeng reverse his pairing in different ways. Baiyu and Foyuan offer new tests of care rather than treating either formula as final. The line names one side of a deliberately reversible teaching contrast.

Senses.Explanation: The question is found in the place of the answer, and the answer in the place of the question. The two clauses make the relation reciprocal. Chuiwan says the formula can leave a person muddled, then works through asking and answering anew. Baishan says that question and answer sometimes meet and sometimes do not after a live shout and blow. Tianan places the line in a verse on everyday speech. Xueguan uses it to read a reply to an emperor, then asks what that reply means. Zide answers a monk with the paired line when asked how to discuss Caoshan prohibitions. The inherited old-master wording is a source family, not the five current voices.

Senses.Explanation: A question-and-answer exchange is the asking-and-answering unit preserved in Chan encounters and records. In Zhaozhou's record, an unnamed monk asks how the master answers if every question-and-answer falls within the thinking faculty; Zhaozhou replies, “Ask.” The expression also labels documentary form: Zhongfeng Mingben's record notes that a question-and-answer was not recorded, and the Record of the Mirror of the School assigns a question-and-answer division the job of removing doubt. The format alone does not establish a successful Chan encounter. Foyan Qingyuan criticizes people who simply take question-and-answer to be the Chan house style. Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen says that a genuine question requires an apt answer and calls a mismatched pair deaf and blind to one another; Yingshan Zhiyin likewise conditions fluent question-and-answer on correctly assessing the exchanges already raised.

The point of the question is the place where a question bears within an exchange, which may itself become the object of a later judgment. Yuanwu Keqin discusses the case in which Huichao asks Fayan what Buddha is and Fayan answers, 'You are Huichao.' Yuanwu lists later explanations, including the claim that 'the point of the question itself is it', and rejects such verbal interpretations. The headword occurs in the words of these unnamed interpreters as Yuanwu reports them. It names where their interpretation locates the answer; Yuanwu's response challenges that interpretation rather than endorsing it. Linji Yixuan describes several ways teachers and students meet as host and guest. In this example, a teacher presents no object or contrived situation but immediately takes away the student's footing at the point of the student's question. If the student stubbornly refuses to let go, Linji calls this 'the host examining the guest'. The phrase identifies the opening supplied by the student's questioning within Linji's described encounter; Huangbo is not the speaker of this passage. Mazu asks Nanquan, who is carrying food, what is in the bucket. Nanquan replies, 'Shut your mouth.' Tianjing Xin then comments that Nanquan does not know the point of Mazu's question and Mazu does not understand the point of Nanquan's answer. He adds that, had they understood, their Jiangxi descendants would not have been swept away. The paired question-point and answer-point mark the two turns that Tianjing is judging, rather than identifying a physical place.

Senses.Explanation: Pinching the eyes to produce flowers names an illusion manufactured by forcing or distorting one's own sight. Pinjixiang Zhixiang and Yingning Zhijing apply it while criticizing inherited displays around Shakyamuni and Mahakasyapa. Zhe'an Jingfan says cultivation and realization can amount to this eye-made display; Yushan Shangsi compares further explanatory speech to it; Foyan Qingyuan warns that seeing matters this way goes astray; and Mingjue Cong rejects taking such appearances as real form. Across these uses, the flowers are not a discovery but an artifact of the attempt to see.
